claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Even in the absence of reaction-diffusion dynamics, actin waves may be described in terms of an active fluid.
claims.source: But even in the absence of reaction-diffusion dynamics, actin waves may be described in terms of an active fluid (Le Goff et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: An active fluid approach does not require any nonlinear biochemistry and solely depends on actin polymerization dynamics, steric repulsion between actin filaments (which tends to align them nematically), and treadmilling.
claims.source: This approach does not require any nonlinear biochemistry and solely depends on actin polymerization dynamics, steric repulsion between actin filaments (which tends to align them nematically), and treadmilling.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the features of a specific modeling approach.

claims.claim: The filaments' alignment destabilizes the isotropic phase and induces transient actin spots or spirals as part of a dynamic pathway toward a polarized phase, which can be either uniform or may consist of a series of actin-wave trains.
claims.source: The filaments' alignment destabilizes the isotropic phase and induces transient actin spots or spirals as part of a dynamic pathway toward a polarized phase, which can be either uniform or may consist of a series of actin-wave trains.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the behavior of the active fluid model.

claims.claim: Models that treat the dynamic actin network at the single-filament level may exhibit wave dynamics on the cell membrane.
claims.source: Models that treat the dynamic actin network at the single-filament level may also exhibit wave dynamics on the cell membrane.

claims.claim: In one of the earliest single-filament models, actin filaments are nucleated by NPFs and are assumed to branch, break, and bind to the membrane.
claims.source: In one of the earliest models, actin filaments are nucleated by NPFs and are assumed to branch, break, and bind to the membrane (Carlsson, 2010).

claims.claim: The Carlsson model includes a negative feedback from F-actin to the NPFs.

claims.evidence: This is a description of the features of a specific model.

claims.claim: Stochastic computations of the Carlsson model display traveling waves, moving patches, as well as fluctuations, but no moving pulses or periodic structures.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Some models combine several modules, including the chemical network of reaction-diffusion equations, in addition to a filament-scale description of the actin network dynamics.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Models that describe the details of the actin network at the level of individual filaments, branching, capping, and cross-linking proteins have the advantage of providing a description that is much closer to the experimental system than the more simplified, reduced models.
claims.source: On the one hand, models that describe the details of the actin network at the level of individual filaments, branching, capping, and cross-linking proteins have the obvious advantage of providing a description that is much closer to the experimental system than the more simplified, reduced models.

results.result: Actin waves are widespread phenomena observed across multiple cell types, characterized by propagating regions of increased F-actin density in the cell cortex. These waves involve complex regulatory networks with multiple feedback loops and are enriched in actin-related proteins and regulatory components.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C9, C19-C23 collectively establish that actin waves are well-documented phenomena across diverse cell types (neutrophils, D. discoideum, X. laevis oocytes, etc.) with consistent structural features. The claims are supported by extensive citations to experimental observations and represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Key mechanistic questions about actin waves remain unresolved, including whether underlying mechanisms are conserved across cell types, which molecular components are essential, and whether waves have specific functions or are byproducts of other processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C12, C24, C26, C39, C187-C188 consistently identify major open questions in the field. These statements accurately reflect current limitations in understanding and are appropriately framed as knowledge gaps rather than resolved findings.

results.result: Mathematical modeling and bifurcation theory are essential tools for understanding actin wave dynamics, particularly for identifying core mechanisms and model-independent principles that cannot be addressed through experimental observation or verbal reasoning alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C13-C15, C190-C196 present a coherent argument for the necessity and utility of mathematical approaches. The claims are supported by citations (C4, C15) and logical reasoning about the limitations of purely experimental or qualitative approaches. This represents the central thesis of the review.

results.result: The FitzHugh-Nagumo model exemplifies successful model reduction, simplifying the four-variable Hodgkin-Huxley model to a two-variable phenomenological model that has proven valuable for understanding excitable and oscillatory dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 are well-supported by citations to established work (Hodgkin and Huxley 1952, Ermentrout and Terman 2010, Tyson and Keener 1988, Meron 1992). This represents a canonical example in the field of mathematical biology.

results.result: Actin waves have been associated with various cellular functions including motility, division, and phagocytosis, though functional roles may vary between cell types and in some cases the functional significance remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C36-C37, C42, C53-C61 are supported by multiple experimental citations showing correlations between actin waves and cellular functions. The claims appropriately acknowledge uncertainty where it exists (C26) while documenting established associations.

results.result: Wave-like actin dynamics have been documented for several decades, beginning with circular dorsal ruffles in the 1970s, with observations expanding to include various wave types across multiple cell types as microscopy techniques improved.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C34 provide a historical account of actin wave observations, supported by citations spanning from the 1970s (Abercrombie et al. 1970) through the 2000s. This represents well-documented scientific history.

results.result: In neutrophils, Hem-1 (a WAVE complex component) exhibits self-activation and negative regulation by F-actin, giving rise to actin waves that show excitable behavior and organize protrusion dynamics at the leading edge.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C109-C112 describe the neutrophil system based on the pioneering work of Weiner et al. 2007. The mechanism (self-activation with F-actin negative feedback) and functional consequences are supported by experimental observations and modeling.

results.result: Signaling components including calcium, phosphoinositides, Rho GTPases, and myosin play important roles in actin wave dynamics, with specific mechanisms varying across cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41, C43-C44 are supported by citations to experimental work showing the involvement of these signaling components. The claims appropriately acknowledge both established roles and remaining uncertainties.

results.result: Ventral actin waves in D. discoideum consist of ring-shaped structures with distinct inner and outer regions characterized by different protein compositions, network architectures, and signaling states, with many dynamic patterns preserved even when actin polymerization is inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C52 describe the detailed structure and composition of D. discoideum actin waves, supported by multiple experimental citations (Bretschneider et al. 2009, Schroth-Diez et al. 2009, Jasnin et al. 2019, etc.). The observation that patterns persist with actin inhibition (C52) is particularly important for understanding wave mechanisms.

results.result: Detailed actin wave models with large sets of coupled equations often have arbitrary parameter values that cannot be uniquely determined from experiments, and their analysis relies mainly on numerical simulations with uncertain robustness to model details.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C65 present a critical assessment of detailed modeling approaches. These are reasonable inferences about the limitations of complex models, supported by citations (C62) and general principles of mathematical modeling.

results.result: Reduced actin wave models aim to identify core mechanisms by removing complexity while maintaining biological interpretation, though some highly simplified models are driven primarily by mathematical intuition with only vague biological interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68, C70-C72 describe the spectrum of model reduction approaches. These represent established modeling strategies in mathematical biology, appropriately distinguishing between mechanistic reduced models and phenomenological 'toy' models.

results.result: Most reduced actin wave models share a common motif: interacting species connected via positive and negative feedback loops creating nonlinear local dynamics, spatially coupled through diffusive transport or mechanical effects, with the key motif being autoactivation coupled to slow negative feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76, C124-C126 identify common structural features across actin wave models. This synthesis is supported by the extensive model review in the manuscript and represents a valid generalization based on established knowledge (C125).

results.result: Experiments with Latrunculin A treatment in D. discoideum demonstrated that neither F-actin nor cAMP are required for wave generation, inspiring a PIP2/PIP3 signaling model where PIP3 negatively regulates PTEN membrane association while PIP2 activates PTEN.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C83 describe the development of the PIP2/PIP3 model based on experimental observations (Arai et al. 2010, Shibata et al. 2012). The experimental evidence and model assumptions are clearly documented with appropriate citations.

results.result: Subsequent experiments revealed that Ras activation is central to wave generation in D. discoideum, with Ras waves affecting PI3K and PIP3 but persisting independently, leading to an extended model incorporating Ras GTPase dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 describe the evolution of understanding based on newer experimental findings (Huang et al. 2013, Nishikawa et al. 2014, Fukushima et al. 2019). This represents appropriate updating of models based on new evidence.

results.result: Excitable network models coupling signaling and cytoskeletal modules have successfully reproduced many experimental observations of actin wave patterns in D. discoideum under diverse conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by citations to the development and application of excitable network models (Xiong et al. 2010, Huang et al. 2013, Miao et al. 2017, 2019). The success in reproducing experimental observations is documented.

results.result: Phase field approaches and generic wave generator models combined with dynamic cell boundaries have been used to study actin waves in deforming cells, successfully capturing observations of cell-to-cell variability, motility phenotypes, and division events in D. discoideum.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C97 describe the application of phase field methods to actin wave modeling, supported by multiple citations (Taniguchi et al. 2013, Knoch et al. 2014, Alonso et al. 2018, Flemming et al. 2020, etc.). The success in capturing diverse phenomena is documented.

results.result: In Xenopus oocytes, waves of Rho and F-actin can be induced by expressing Ect2 (GEF) and RGA3/4 (GAP), with F-actin following Rho activity. A model incorporating autocatalytic Rho activation and F-actin-mediated inactivation reproduces these dynamics, which have been reconstituted in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C106 describe the Xenopus oocyte system based on extensive experimental work (Bement et al. 2015, Michaud et al. 2021, 2022, Landino et al. 2021). The in vitro reconstitution (C103-C106) provides particularly strong evidence for the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Analysis of disordered wave patterns in starfish oocytes using the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation suggests that observed spiral wave properties are generic, model-independent features.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by citation to Tan et al. 2020. The use of the CGL equation to identify generic features is an appropriate mathematical approach for systems near oscillation onset.

results.result: In C. elegans embryos, Rho leads to actin assembly via formins, with negative feedback from the Rho GAP RGA-3/4 recruited by F-actin. Perturbations to anillin or formin affect the observed patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 describe the C. elegans system based on experimental observations (Michaux et al. 2018, Yao et al. 2022). The mechanism differs from other systems in using formins rather than Arp2/3, representing important biological diversity.

results.result: Rho activates myosin contraction, and recent models incorporate feedback where actomyosin-generated stress feeds back to Rho activation, though many models do not address this feature.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 acknowledge a known biological connection (Rho-myosin) and note that most models reviewed do not incorporate this, with one exception (Staddon et al. 2022). This is an appropriate critical observation.

results.result: Alternative models assign autocatalysis to F-actin itself (e.g., via Arp2/3 branching) with an additional inhibitor, ranging from simple two-component models amenable to mathematical analysis to more complex variants including coronin-mediated disassembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C123 describe F-actin-centric models, supported by citations (Yochelis et al. 2020, 2022, Bernitt et al. 2017, Wasnik and Mukhopadhyay 2014). The range from simple to complex variants is appropriately documented.

results.result: Models incorporating detailed actin network structure with polarity fields show that waves are affected by treadmilling-induced flows, but the core wave-generating mechanism involves cooperative NPF binding and negative feedback from actin filament density.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 describe detailed network models (Dreher et al. 2014, Doubrovinski and Kruse 2011, Liu et al. 2021). The identification of the core mechanism despite additional complexity is an important finding.

results.result: Active fluid models can describe actin wave dynamics, with some requiring only actin polymerization, steric repulsion, and treadmilling (without nonlinear biochemistry), where filament alignment destabilizes the isotropic phase leading to spots, spirals, or wave trains.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 describe active fluid approaches (Camley et al. 2013, Le Goff et al. 2016). The ability to generate waves without biochemical nonlinearity (C134-C135) represents an alternative mechanism worth noting.

results.result: Single-filament level models incorporating nucleation, branching, and membrane binding can exhibit wave dynamics, with early models showing traveling waves and patches, and later models with cooperative NPF interactions producing more complex patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C144 describe filament-level models (Carlsson 2010, Holmes et al. 2012, Enculescu et al. 2010, Gholami et al. 2012, Nonaka et al. 2011). The progression from simpler to more complex models is appropriately documented.

results.result: Detailed filament-level models provide descriptions closer to experimental systems but require greater computational resources and are not amenable to mathematical analysis for obtaining mechanistic insights.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C147 present a balanced assessment of the tradeoffs in detailed modeling. This represents reasonable inference about the limitations and advantages of different modeling approaches.

results.result: Cell geometry and boundary dynamics can affect actin waves by altering local densities, diffusive transport, and through boundary curvature effects that can trap peaks or accelerate dynamics. Most models use 2D projections with closed contours, with some extending to 3D.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C155 describe geometric effects on actin waves, supported by citations (Wei 1999, Iron and Ward 2000, Marée et al. 2012, Camley et al. 2017, and others). These represent established phenomena in reaction-diffusion systems.

results.result: Cell shape changes generate cytoplasmic fluid flows that advect soluble components and affect wave dynamics. Models incorporating these effects are computationally intensive, though alternative descriptions as active poroelastic media have been proposed.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C159 describe fluid flow effects, supported by citations (Campbell and Bagchi 2018, Radszuweit et al. 2013, Kulawiak et al. 2019). The computational challenges and alternative approaches are appropriately noted.

results.result: Curvature-sensitive proteins create bidirectional coupling between actin waves and membrane curvature: actin polymerization deforms membranes, and resulting curvature affects actin regulator dynamics. Convex proteins induce positive feedback through protrusive forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C167 describe curvature-mediated feedback, supported by citations (Tamemoto and Noguchi 2020, 2021, Wu et al. 2018, Gov 2018, Marée et al. 2012, Camley et al. 2017). The bidirectional coupling is well-documented.

results.result: Negative feedback in curvature-mediated systems can arise through myosin-driven retraction creating concave curvature, mixtures of convex/concave proteins, external confinement, or Ca2+-ion flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C171 describe multiple mechanisms for negative feedback, each supported by citations (Shlomovitz and Gov 2007, Peleg et al. 2011, Naoz and Gov 2020, Veksler and Gov 2009). The diversity of mechanisms is appropriately documented.

results.result: Membrane tension provides another mechano-chemical feedback route: actin-driven protrusions increase tension, which inhibits actin polymerization directly or through release of inhibitory factors (PLD2, mTORC2). This feedback is incorporated in models of cell-edge waves.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C179 describe tension-mediated feedback, supported by citations (Wu and Liu 2021, Houk et al. 2012, Diz-Muñoz et al. 2013, 2016, Barnhart et al. 2017, Tarama et al. 2022). The mechanisms and modeling applications are well-documented.

results.result: Mechano-chemical models fall into distinct classes: those treating geometry/confinement as downstream effects, and those where mechanical forces are integral to wave-generating feedback. It's not always clear which route underlies experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C180-C186 provide a classification of mechano-chemical models and acknowledge uncertainty about which mechanisms operate in vivo. This represents appropriate critical synthesis of the modeling literature.

results.result: The challenge in modeling is balancing biological realism with mathematical tractability. Model validity depends on both data fitting and predictive ability. Simple models amenable to analysis can reveal model-independent mechanisms, while bifurcation theory provides a framework to identify core building blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C196 present the authors' perspective on modeling philosophy and the role of mathematical theory. These represent reasonable inferences about modeling principles, supported by the extensive review of the field.

results.result: Poincaré demonstrated limitations of linear mechanics in predicting three-body motion, founding chaos theory and bifurcation theory. Nonlinear systems differ from linear ones in admitting multiple coexisting solutions with important stability properties. Bifurcation theory is the most powerful approach for analyzing nonlinear PDEs.
results.evaluation: Claims C197-C203 provide historical and conceptual background on bifurcation theory, supported by citation to Poincaré 1885. These represent established mathematical history and principles.

results.result: Bifurcation refers to branching of solutions as control parameters vary, corresponding to qualitative changes in system behavior. Bifurcation diagrams map solution existence and stability, with specific mathematical rules governing solution appearance (in pairs) and stability exchange.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C211 define fundamental concepts in bifurcation theory, supported by citation to Poincaré 1885 and established mathematical knowledge. These represent standard definitions in dynamical systems theory.

results.result: Pitchfork bifurcations create bistability, while Hopf bifurcations generate oscillations (ubiquitous in biology). Higher co-dimension bifurcations require multiple control parameters and exhibit richer dynamics, potentially revealing core model building blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C212-C218 describe specific bifurcation types and their properties. These represent standard bifurcation theory, with biological examples appropriately cited. The connection to model design (C218) is a reasonable inference.

results.result: Optogenetic repolarization experiments in macrophages were analyzed using PDE bifurcation methods, revealing distinct response regimes and signatures depending on the underlying polarization model. Cells with mutually antagonistic GTPases show simpler repolarization routes than single-GTPase systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C219-C225 describe application of bifurcation analysis to experimental data, supported by citations (O'Neill et al. 2016, Buttenschön and Edelstein-Keshet 2022, Holmes and Edelstein-Keshet 2016, Mori et al. 2008). This demonstrates the utility of the mathematical approach.

results.result: Full PDE bifurcation analysis has not been applied to most actin wave models, though local perturbation analysis (LPA) has been used to explore parameter effects on pattern formation, with predictions in principle testable through manipulation of GEFs and GAPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C226-C228 identify a gap in the field (lack of full bifurcation analysis) while noting the use of LPA shortcuts (Holmes et al. 2012, Mata et al. 2013). The statement about testability (C228) is a reasonable inference.

results.result: CDRs were initially assumed to be excitable waves based on collision annihilation, but observations of boundary reflections challenged this. Bifurcation analysis combined with experiments revealed CDRs are bistable fronts, explaining both reflections and different propagation speeds of expanding/contracting rings.
results.evaluation: Claims C229-C239 describe a complete research story from hypothesis to resolution, supported by citations (Zeng et al. 2011, Bernitt et al. 2015, 2017). The experimental evidence (C233) and theoretical analysis (C234-C239) converge to support the bistable interpretation. This exemplifies successful integration of experiment and theory.

results.result: Understanding CDR dynamics may help explain links to cancer progression by providing a framework for understanding roles of cytoskeletal components and signaling factors.
results.evaluation: Claim C240 is explicitly framed as speculation about future applications ('may, in future'). While supported by citations suggesting CDR-cancer links (Orth and McNiven 2006, Hoon et al. 2012, Itoh and Hasegawa 2013), the causal connection remains to be established.
